articles.title: The Incredible, Elegant DNA Repair System Makes Gene Editing Work
articles.author: Annie Melchor
articles.body_markdown:
## Introduction

Humans have debated the meaning of life for many millennia, but from evolution’s perspective, it is simple: Preserve the genome. Of course, mutation is allowed, as is the genetic mixing and matching of sexual reproduction, to create variety and evolutionary diversity. But we all exist because a viable lineage of DNA has persisted for 4 billion years. The genome’s policy is typically, “If the code works, don’t change it.”

You’d think, then, that cells would keep their DNA under lock and key, protected from the elements like the precious blueprint it is. But this isn’t possible. DNA is a working document. Cells need near-constant access to these instructions for making the molecules required by life. The huge, complex molecular structure is therefore exposed to nonstop assault by the by-products of everyday cellular metabolism, as well as environmental factors, such as radiation (including ultraviolet and X-ray), alcohol, pesticides, and more.

“DNA damage occurs all the time,” said Björn Schumacher, a molecular biologist at the University of Cologne. “[DNA] contains all the information for building a cell, building an organism, maintaining cells and tissues, and all that — but yet it is surprisingly unstable.”

He estimates that some cells endure up to 100,000 DNA damage events every day. “Damage to the DNA is the default,” he said. These events can injure sections of the DNA molecule — or, worse, break the strand in half. Even minor DNA damage risks changing or destroying the essential instructions a cell needs to operate, which can make cells malfunction, die, or become cancerous.

However, many of those tens of thousands of daily lesions get repaired quickly. Cells have native repair mechanisms that recognize and replace faulty DNA before lasting damage and dysfunction set in. In fact, the ability to repair damaged or broken DNA had to evolve at essentially the same time as DNA, Schumacher said, “because you cannot have stable genetic information without DNA repair.”

These mechanisms are essential not only to the evolutionary lineage of all known life, but also to promising technologies to treat genetic diseases. Scientists and doctors who experiment with gene editing must rely on DNA’s natural self-editing and repair tools to insert, delete, or mutate genes to study and treat disease.

So perhaps instead of a master blueprint protected behind glass, it’s better to imagine DNA as a beloved cookbook that is constantly in use. While it’s open on the kitchen counter, it’s bound to get splattered with sauce — or even have a page ripped. But spills can be wiped off. Torn pages can be taped up. And a smear obscuring an odd ingredient might even improve a recipe.

## Do the Twist

To understand how DNA gets damaged so easily, we need to see its structure, beyond the impossible elegance of the double helix. Most DNA is packed into chromosomes, dense structures formed by long, delicate filaments of DNA wrapped tightly around proteins. If you were to unwrap the DNA and untwist its double helix, you’d see a ladder made of nucleotides: the building blocks of DNA.

A single DNA strand — one side rail and half of each rung — encodes a specific arrangement of the four nucleotides, also known as bases. Each is a complex molecule represented by a single letter: A, T, G, or C. Across from it is a backup on the opposite, complementary strand, made up of each nucleotide’s natural partner (A’s partner is T, and G’s is C). The “rungs” of the DNA ladder are held together with relatively weak, transient bonds that allow the helix to be opened and closed like a zipper, so enzymes can access, read, and copy the code.

“[DNA has] all that clever structure to it, to enable it to come apart and replicate,” said Penny Jeggo, a molecular biologist who is now emeritus faculty at the University of Sussex. “But a consequence of [that structure] is that it’s sensitive to damage, and unlike proteins or RNA, it actually matters if it gets damaged.”

Even though DNA is precious, it also needs to be constantly accessed to provide the instructions for making the cells’ proteins. And it’s important to remember that the enzymes don’t “read” it from a distance. Every step is a tactile, chemical process. Like toddlers, enzymes physically touch, interact with, and occasionally change the DNA to work with it.

“[DNA is] a working molecule,” said Maria Jasin, a molecular biologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. “So just by its nature, DNA is going to be subject to chemical forces that will modify it.”

When that modification — let’s call it what it is, damage — affects just a single nucleotide base, a process called base excision repair sends in enzymes to pop the incorrect or injured molecule off the strand and replace it with an undamaged one. Sometimes the jobs are heftier, such as when ultraviolet radiation or carcinogenic chemicals cause a base to fuse with an adjacent one, creating a bulky distortion in the DNA backbone. In this case, enzymes snip out entire nucleotide chunks from the problematic strand and replace them using the complementary strand as a template — a process called nucleotide excision repair.

The most devastating DNA injury of all is a double-strand break. When this happens, the genome is severed into two pieces, resulting in a potentially catastrophic loss of information from both copies of the code. In these cases, the cell deploys the full DNA damage response. An intricate network of more than 500 proteins senses the damage and quickly intervenes to stabilize the damaged segments. It also issues a temporary moratorium on any DNA replication or RNA transcription to prevent the cell from using faulty code.

Double-strand breaks are dangerous. A cell might opt to self-destruct rather than risk perpetuating serious mutations. However, most double-strand breaks can be repaired through one of two main pathways.

“One is beautiful in its simplicity,” Jeggo said, “and the other one is just as beautiful or elegant in its complexity.”

The simpler pathway, and the one used more commonly by human cells, is called nonhomologous end joining. Proteins stabilize the free-floating ends of the DNA, clear out any damaged nucleotides, trim the ends so they are flush, and then basically stick them back together. Some nucleotides are irrevocably lost, and mutations may arise as a result, but for most cells, it gets the job done.

The other, more accurate pathway for restoring double-strand breaks is called homologous recombination. It’s available only during cell division, after DNA has replicated but before the cell divides. In this moment, the nucleus holds two identical copies of each chromosome, known as sister chromatids. If a double-strand break occurs in this brief window, any lost code can be filled in by its sister through homologous recombination. Proteins choreograph an elegant pas de deux where a damaged DNA strand intertwines with the complementary strand from its undamaged sister. The intact strand serves as a perfect template for copying over any nucleotides that may have been lost.

## Putting Nature to Work

Homologous recombination is not a “good enough” form of repair. It is so accurate that scientists have harnessed it for gene editing. In 1994, Jasin’s team intentionally introduced a double-strand break in the mouse genome. In place of a sister chromatid, her team provided DNA with a new gene in it, surrounded by sequences designed to coax the cell to stitch it in using homologous recombination. Indeed, the new gene was added to the existing DNA sequence right where the strand had been broken.

Jasin’s team was not the first to edit genes using homologous recombination, but they showed that the process was immensely more efficient if the DNA strands had been broken first. However, their approach had a major limitation: The enzyme that broke the DNA strands, called an endonuclease, could only make a cut at a specific DNA sequence. For every editing project, the endonuclease would have to be redesigned to match its target gene — a significant effort.

That burden was lifted in 2012 with the realization that CRISPR-Cas, a bacterial immune system, had massive potential as a gene-editing tool. Cas is an endonuclease that finds its cutting site by a different method: A piece of RNA guides it to the target DNA segment. Because synthesizing a strand of RNA is far easier than designing an endonuclease, CRISPR-Cas enabled researchers to make cuts virtually anywhere in the genome.

This approach is a kind of genetic surgery. It makes incisions in the DNA with scalpel-like precision and relies on the body’s natural mechanisms to heal it. But it does this on a molecular scale, so its intervention is more fundamental than what the most skilled surgeon could produce. Like earlier tools, CRISPR-Cas relies on the cell’s native DNA repair machinery to put things back together with the edited genes. Some researchers use homologous recombination to add in a desired gene sequence while others take advantage of nonhomologous end joining to intentionally introduce mutations.

More recently, an emerging gene-editing technology called base editing lets researchers target and change individual bases without introducing a double-strand break. For treating human conditions caused by single mutations, base editing may be far safer than CRISPR-Cas, since it doesn’t require double-strand breaks. Instead, it competes with and manipulates the base excision repair process to change a single nucleotide. Indeed, in 2025, it was used to treat a baby with a rare genetic condition; a personalized gene-editing cocktail fixed his precise mutation. However, a 2026 study of base editing reported that the technique is not precise enough to be safely used in human embryos.

Researchers will continue to leverage the DNA repair mechanisms that evolution has developed to create research tools and possibly even cure challenging genetic diseases. But, as with surgery, there will always be some risk involved. DNA works as a conveyor of life’s instructions because it is imperfect enough to enable evolution. And that means that imperfections will appear in our attempts to work with it, too.

articles.title: A Former DOGE Operative Won a Federal Contract. Then Things Got Messy
articles.author: Vittoria Elliott
articles.body_markdown:
Yet another former member of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) appears to have exited the government only to return as a contractor.

In September, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) put out a call for a contract worth $200,000 for “modernization discovery, prototyping, and implementation-planning engagement.” Four days later, the department closed the bidding process and awarded the contract to Yat Choi LLC, a company owned by a former Airbnb engineer and Canadian citizen named Yat Choi, whose company also goes by the name GovMaxxing.

At the time, Choi had left his role at the National Design Studio (NDS)—the group tasked with redesigning government websites—just a few weeks prior. Before that, Choi worked at DOGE.

The bid was for a project set to run for a little under six months, and the contract was awarded as sole-source, meaning that it did not go through a normal competitive bidding process. In the documentation announcing the award, HHS justified this decision by saying that its “market research and source rationale found that conventional consulting firms generally would need to assemble a multidisciplinary team or obtain additional technical resources” to provide the required skills around “business-process modernization, artificial intelligence, automation, technical architecture, and rapid prototyping.”

In October, a company called CoA Solutions lodged what’s known as a bid protest with the Government Accountability Office (GAO) contesting the agency’s decision to award the contract to Choi. CoA Solutions is a small business that builds AI software for the government and received another contract with the Treasury Department in 2024.

Ari Perez, the CEO of CoA Solutions, tells WIRED that his company made a bid below the $200,000 award price, and it proposed two experts doing the work full-time, including Perez himself.

Perez says that CoA asked HHS for an explanation of the award on October 8 and, when it did not receive one, filed its protest with the GAO the next day. Perez says that his company’s sole contestation was about how the bids were evaluated by HHS, not about Choi or his work with NDS.

“I'm a service-disabled veteran. I've served this government since I was 17 at West Point. At the US Digital Service I helped deliver for veterans at the VA, and later I worked on asylum and immigration systems at DHS. I started CoA to keep doing impactful government work,” says Perez. “We want to win on merit, and if HHS reopens it, we'll bid again.”

According to CoA, in response to the bid protest, HHS terminated the award to Choi and canceled the call for contractors. With the cancellation, the GAO dismissed the protest without investigating it further. A GAO spokesperson referred WIRED to HHS.

“HHS remains committed to modernizing its systems to improve efficiency and better serve the American people,” says HHS spokesperson Grace Davis Jamison. “Following a bid protest challenging the award, HHS voluntarily took corrective action, terminating the contract at no cost to the government and canceling the solicitation.”

Choi’s role in the US government has not been exactly clear. In his bio on X, Choi writes that he was part of both DOGE and NDS, and said in a post that he was recruited by billionaire Elon Musk and Joe Gebbia, Airbnb’s cofounder, to help modernize the retirement system at the Office of Personnel Management (OPM). Gebbia now leads NDS, which was created after Musk left government and which has served as a landing pad for several DOGE members, including Edward “Big Balls” Coristine.

In December 2025, Choi contributed to a blog on the NDS website about automating the federal retirement system. But on his LinkedIn, Choi lists himself as a senior technologist at OPM. On November 5, just two days after Republicans lost the midterm elections, Choi announced in a post on X that he had left OPM and was launching his company, GovMaxxing, through which he plans to continue to contract with the government. GovMaxxing operates as Yat Choi LLC federally.

In response to questions from WIRED about his role in government, Choi says that he “was recruited to support federal modernization efforts and subsequently onboarded as an OPM contractor.” There, Choi says, he “contributed to modernization efforts associated with DOGE and subsequently NDS. I was not, and have never been, a federal government employee.” Choi claims he left OPM in mid-August, though OPM did not respond to questions confirming whether this was the case. “I began actively pursuing the contracting opportunity after my engagement with OPM ended,” says Choi.

Choi confirmed that he is a Canadian citizen and a “lawful permanent resident” of the US. Foreigners are not generally allowed to hold full-time roles in government or serve as special government employees. The rules are more flexible for contractors. During the height of DOGE’s activity, a close Musk ally, Baris Akis, was prevented from joining the group as a special government employee because he is a Turkish citizen, according to The Atlantic. Akis, however, continued to serve as a recruiter for the group.

On his website, Choi labels the “client” for his work in government as “US Office of Personnel Management / DOGE / National Design Studio” and describes himself as the “modernization lead.” However, documents indicate that Choi’s company was not registered in the state of New York until April 2026, and in the System for Award Management, the procurement website where US government contractors bid, there are no other contracts for Choi’s work. “None of my work at OPM was performed through my LLC. My website references my prior professional experience at OPM and does not attribute that work to my company,” says Choi.

Choi says that the HHS contract was for a “separate modernization discovery project. It was not a continuation of any work with OPM, DOGE, or NDS.”

According to the code of federal regulations, except in very specific circumstances, government contracts cannot be awarded to government employees or to organizations they fully or partially own. But Jessica Tillipman, associate dean for government procurement law studies at George Washington University, says that even though Choi was not a regular government employee, the fact that he was part of DOGE and NDS, whose work has spanned across government agencies, could create the appearance of a conflict of interest with regard to the HHS contract. “The baseline posture of the federal acquisition regulation is to strictly avoid conflicts of interest or even the appearance of them,” says Tillipman. “So agencies all have a duty, and the contracting teams have a duty, to make sure that they are considering these things when they're awarding these contracts.”

Choi tells WIRED that HHS “initiated contact and expressed interest” in his “modernization experience” before the call for bids was announced. HHS did not respond to questions about whether the bid had been written specifically for him.

Tillipman notes that while the government may sometimes create a contracting opportunity designed for a specific person or company, “it’s generally niche or highly specialized work." Tillipman says that the fact that there were 75 bids placed on the contract indicates that this is “not a unique service.” She notes that the government’s justification for a sole-source contract is “thin.” “Usually, when there's only one responsible source, there's a technical reason,” she says. This could be something like a special tool that is not interoperable with outside software, or when there is only one company that can provide a specific service or that makes a certain physical part that might be used for weapons or specialized machinery.

On the GovMaxxing website, Choi notes that potential government clients can work with the company as a prime contractor or “subcontract through one of our partner primes your agency may already be working with.” Unlike prime contracts, there is no way to publicly see which subcontractor a prime contractor works with. Choi declined to name the companies or current “prime” contractors he subcontracts under.

But Tillipman says that even if Choi were to take on another version of the HHS contract for a subcontractor, similar questions could still be raised within the agency and externally should it ever come to light. “In certain instances, your subcontractors’ conflicts can be imputed to the prime contractor,” she says. “The whole thing is highly irregular overall.”

Choi is not the only former DOGE or NDS member who appears to be hoping to benefit from federal contracts after leaving the government. Earlier this year, WIRED reported that Ethan Shaotran, one of the young engineers who formed the early core of DOGE, had started a defense tech startup. The startup has been listed on the System for Award Management since April. Former DOGE members Jack Stein, Gavin Kliger, Luke Farritor, and Marko Elez launched an AI defense technology company called Cathedral, which has been listed on the System for Award Management since July. Neither have received “prime” contracts with any federal agency, but whether they have been taken on as subcontractors to other prime contractors is unclear.

Despite the HHS contract’s cancellation, Choi appears undeterred. Earlier this week, following the nationwide grounding of flights by the Federal Aviation Administration, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called for funding to modernize air traffic control in a post on X. In response, Choi wrote, “Secretary Duffy, I’m the DOGE engineer who led the modernization of federal retirement processing at OPM last year … I’ve since started a company to work with more agencies, and we’d love to help with the FAA’s modernization efforts. Put us in, coach!”

But Jessica Tillipman, associate dean for government procurement law studies at George Washington University, says that even though Choi was not a regular government employee, the fact that he was part of DOGE and NDS, whose work has spanned across government agencies, could create the appearance of a conflict of interest with regard to the HHS contract. “The baseline posture of the federal acquisition regulation is to strictly avoid conflicts of interest or even the appearance of them,” says Tillipman. “So agencies all have a duty, and the contracting teams have a duty, to make sure that they are considering these things when they're awarding these contracts.”

Choi tells WIRED that HHS “initiated contact and expressed interest” in his “modernization experience” before the call for bids was announced. HHS did not respond to questions about whether the bid had been written specifically for him.

Tillipman notes that while the government may sometimes create a contracting opportunity designed for a specific person or company, “it’s generally niche or highly specialized work." Tillipman says that the fact that there were 75 bids placed on the contract indicates that this is “not a unique service.” She notes that the government’s justification for a sole-source contract is “thin.” “Usually, when there's only one responsible source, there's a technical reason,” she says. This could be something like a special tool that is not interoperable with outside software, or when there is only one company that can provide a specific service or that makes a certain physical part that might be used for weapons or specialized machinery.

On the GovMaxxing website, Choi notes that potential government clients can work with the company as a prime contractor or “subcontract through one of our partner primes your agency may already be working with.” Unlike prime contracts, there is no way to publicly see which subcontractor a prime contractor works with. Choi declined to name the companies or current “prime” contractors he subcontracts under.

But Tillipman says that even if Choi were to take on another version of the HHS contract for a subcontractor, similar questions could still be raised within the agency and externally should it ever come to light. “In certain instances, your subcontractors’ conflicts can be imputed to the prime contractor,” she says. “The whole thing is highly irregular overall.”

Choi is not the only former DOGE or NDS member who appears to be hoping to benefit from federal contracts after leaving the government. Earlier this year, WIRED reported that Ethan Shaotran, one of the young engineers who formed the early core of DOGE, had started a defense tech startup. The startup has been listed on the System for Award Management since April. Former DOGE members Jack Stein, Gavin Kliger, Luke Farritor, and Marko Elez launched an AI defense technology company called Cathedral, which has been listed on the System for Award Management since July. Neither have received “prime” contracts with any federal agency, but whether they have been taken on as subcontractors to other prime contractors is unclear.

Despite the HHS contract’s cancellation, Choi appears undeterred. Earlier this week, following the nationwide grounding of flights by the Federal Aviation Administration, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called for funding to modernize air traffic control in a post on X. In response, Choi wrote, “Secretary Duffy, I’m the DOGE engineer who led the modernization of federal retirement processing at OPM last year … I’ve since started a company to work with more agencies, and we’d love to help with the FAA’s modernization efforts. Put us in, coach!”

articles.title: Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
articles.author: Joel Rose
articles.body_markdown:
EVERGREEN, Colo. — Joan Spalding has driven the steep, winding road that leads to her house outside Denver for more than 50 years. But these days, the 89-year-old barely touches the steering wheel or the pedals.

Instead she tells the car where she wants to go, and presses a button on the large touch-screen in the dashboard of her Tesla Model Y.

"I just get in and go," Spalding says.

For all practical purposes, the car appears to be driving itself, navigating confidently on twisting roads through postcard valleys full of juniper and ponderosa pine.

"Now this is probably one of the narrowest roads," Spalding says, as the car pulls onto a dirt track that can barely fit two cars side by side, with a steep drop off to one side.

The Tesla handles the tight turns gracefully, even stopping to let an SUV squeeze by in the other lane.

Spalding was skeptical at first of what Tesla officially calls Full-Self Driving (Supervised), often abbreviated as FSD. It's a subscription service that drivers pay for, usually $99 dollars per month.

That was, until she saw what it could do.

"When I was driving," Spalding said, "I saw that the kind of things that it did were safer than what I would do."

There are more older drivers on the road than ever, and families often struggle with the question of when it's time to stop driving. Now, seniors are using emerging technology to stay behind the wheel longer, specifically automated systems made by Tesla. But safety experts worry the company may be over-selling what its cars can do.

"It's not a technology that I would drive with. It's not a technology that I would suggest that my loved ones use. I think it has a few safety gaps that just make me uncomfortable," said Bryan Reimer, a research scientist at MIT, who studies how drivers interact with technology.

It's hard to know exactly how many seniors are using Tesla's automated driving system, but the numbers may be growing. Overall, Tesla says FSD has more than 1.7 million active subscriptions, an increase of 67% from a year ago. If the car-maker knows how many of those subscribers are seniors, it isn't saying.

Riding along with Joan Spalding, it's easy to understand the appeal for older drivers. The car gives her mobility and freedom that she wouldn't have otherwise.

Before she got her Tesla, Spalding had gotten into a number of minor fender benders. Then, two years ago, she was in a serious crash while she was trying to make a left turn.

"I made a wrong decision. I wasn't focusing on what I should be doing … I was lucky," she said. "But I realized then that my abilities were not where I wanted them to be."

Her son Mike Spalding had known for a while that his mother's driving was getting worse. He was already driving a Tesla, and it was his idea to get one for her.

"It would be safer for mom if she was in a wreck because it's got all kinds of safety features. And then safer for people around her if we didn't have any more crashes. I've been driving one for years, and so I'd experimented with the Full Self-Driving and saw what it could do," Spalding said. "It's better than me."

Tesla agrees. The company claims that FSD is up to nine times safer than human driving. Tesla doesn't release much data about FSD, so it's impossible to independently verify whether its safety claims are true, Reimer said. He concedes Tesla's technology is impressive and is getting better all the time, but says it's not a replacement for a human driver — at least, not yet.

"Tesla has continually over-promised and under-delivered," Reimer said. "Full self-driving is not full self-driving, but yet the name feels so real."

If you read the fine print, FSD is not fully autonomous. The company always uses its full title — FSD (Supervised) — in official communications, to underscore the point. The driver is supposed to be paying attention at all times, in case the car encounters a situation FSD can't handle.

The problem, according to safety experts, is that human drivers tend to get complacent.

"It's good enough, often enough, where people go, 'The next time I'm in this similar situation, I know how it's going to behave,'" said Alexandra Mueller, a senior research scientist at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, the nonprofit funded by the insurance industry.

But Mueller worries older drivers won't be ready or able to take control of the car in an emergency.

"This can be a huge problem," she said. "Ultimately it is very unsafe if you have drivers who are not fully competent due to age-related impairments or decline."

Tesla did not reply to requests for comment.

The company has not said exactly how many senior drivers are using FSD to stay on the road longer, or even if that's something Tesla is tracking. But the company's CEO, Elon Musk, has encouraged the practice.

In a recent post on his social media platform X, Musk said that "Tesla self-driving gives mobility to seniors." Several times, he's amplified a video from a YouTube channel called TFLEV, featuring a 98-year-old man, who just bought his first Tesla.

"It has not made a mistake. And I've been driving it probably two or three months and it's not made an error in its driving, " the driver, Larry Dimmock, said in the video. "In fact, the other day it stopped. A chipmunk was crossing the road and there was no other traffic and it did not run over the chipmunk."

Musk reposted the video last month, saying, "At Tesla, we even care about the chipmunks." The clip has been viewed more than 3.5 million times.

"My moment of fame, I guess," Dimmock joked in an interview with NPR.

Dimmock says he's owned dozens of cars in his life, starting with a Ford Model A. He says he's still a pretty good driver at 98 — but not as good as his Tesla.

"I feel safer riding with this auto system than I do driving or riding with anybody. It's just been flawless," Dimmock said. "I'll get in the car and go somewhere, otherwise, I probably wouldn't."

For Joan Spalding in Colorado, it's more than just a question of convenience. She says FSD is allowing her to live independently in the house that she and her late husband built more than 50 years ago.

"I love the solitude of being in that place and being by myself," she said.

Without the mobility that FSD gives her, Spalding said, she would likely have to find another place to live where she wouldn't need to drive.

"I'd have to move," she said. "This way, I think I can drive it for as long as I want to. I don't see any reason why not."

articles.title: The Feds Left Iowans in the Dark About Plans to Blow Up Tons of Lead
articles.author: Molly Taft
articles.body_markdown:
On October 26, Charles Massner, the mayor of Mediapolis, Iowa, got an email from the US Army. It described “an intentional, controlled detonation” of “a quantity of degraded lead azide … in the near future” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, some 20 miles south of Mediapolis.

The email, which was reviewed by WIRED, provided no details about when this explosion would happen, how much material the explosion would destroy, or what steps officials should take to protect the public from a possible toxic fallout. But it did request that public officials allow for environmental testing on public lands before and after the event, which the town granted in a November 2 meeting.

Massner says the next time he heard anything was early last week, when the Army published a press release on its website saying it would explode the lead azide in just a few days. That press release included a map of potential exposure from the blast. Mediapolis was directly in the path of exposure, covered in a reddish-yellow cloud with a hot pink border.

“There was really no communication, so to speak, other than what was on their website,” he says.

Massner wasn’t alone in being caught off guard. The sudden announcement that the Army would be exploding 9,500 pounds of lead azide with seemingly little to no notice caught nearly all of Iowa by surprise. Governor Kim Reynolds’ office said last week that they’d learned about the explosion the same way Massner did: via the press release sent out by the Army on November 15.

Now, despite a court order blocking the detonation, the Army announced late Sunday night that it plans to blow up the lead azide on Wednesday, a day before the Thanksgiving holiday. Many Iowans are left with more questions than answers. Iowa’s unofficial state subreddit is filled with posts from people trying to plan holiday travel and safety around the event, which has switched dates twice in the past week. One local official in the path of a potential fallout told WIRED on Friday that she was leaving the area and staying at a hotel with her immunocompromised child.

Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the University of Iowa who has studied exposure to lead in his laboratory, says his lab has been “deluged with concerns,” with everyone from pediatricians to parents to people who run cleaning facilities and are worried about their staff exposure reaching out. Like most Iowans, Thorne also heard about the explosion from the Army’s press release.

“My first reaction was, They’re going to do what?” he says.

The 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at the Middletown site have been there for more than 20 years. In March, according to a document released by the Army on November 18, the material was officially labeled hazardous waste, and officials began looking into how to dispose of it. In a court filing published Saturday, the Army says that there is an “immediate risk” of the material exploding by itself after temperatures drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit. It is now invoking emergency powers to detonate the barrels by November 24.

“In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion,” the filing states.

The Army did not immediately respond to a list of questions sent by WIRED.

The Army does seem to have looked into other options besides blowing up the azide. The New York Times reported Friday that the Army awarded a contract in late March to a private company to handle cleaning up the chemicals onsite. However, that contract was pulled two months later; the company told the Times that the Army did not give a reason for changing its mind on the cleanup. A contracting officer in the Army told the company that the Army’s decision to pursue detonation “was not based on deficiencies” with the company’s science.

In a letter sent to Governor Reynolds on Friday, the EPA Region 7 administrator said that the agency only learned that the material had degraded to a dangerous state in March. The letter also listed a number of strategies the EPA had considered besides detonation, including chemical cleanup, which also risked causing an explosion.

The Army has blown up expired munitions before, although not at the scale of what it plans to do in Iowa. Thorne says that any exposure to lead from the explosion is expected to be “quite a bit lower” than lead exposures in communities exposed to legacy pollution sources. But “there is no safe level for lead, especially for young children,” he says.

The Army did have some public meetings and communications in late October with officials in Middletown, where the explosion will take place and where it has recommended temporary evacuation measures for some neighborhoods. But it’s not clear why its initial direct outreach around public health didn’t extend to towns in potential fallout ranges for a blast, including Mediapolis, beyond asking for permission to test soil samples. (The Army did include recommended public health measures in its November 15 press release.)

Thorne, a former chair of the EPA’s Science Advisory Board, says that a successful public health outreach program has lots of opportunity for public engagement for all affected areas.

“You have public meetings. You answer questions. You have extensive Q&A and FAQs, and you have people speaking to why this is the only choice, what are the burdens, and some kind of a cost-benefit comparison between the options, and then you roll it out through the media, through social media, through many ways,” he says. “Best practice is not what they’ve done—I think this is closer to worst practice, from a public health perspective.”

For his part, Massner, Mediapolis’s mayor, said on Friday that he planned to take “standard precautions” and follow the Army’s public health recommendations. (The Army has not released fallout modeling for a Wednesday explosion, but if winds carry the material south, it would be possible for Mediapolis to no longer be in the affected zone.) But Messner says he understands why people in his town were freaked out.

“What people saw was the map they drew, which showed a [red] cloud going over everybody’s head. I don’t think that was the intent of the map,” he laughs. “When you see a map covered in red, you’re supposed to run for shelter immediately—your life is in danger.”

articles.title: What’s really driving the Ebola outbreak?
articles.author: Sanidhya Sharma
articles.body_markdown:
For Marie-Roseline Bélizaire, a typical day starts around 6 A.M. at a health center in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where she pores over freshly confirmed Ebola cases that have come in overnight. From then on, the work is nonstop: she calls dozens of provinces, visits health centers, supervises contact tracing, trains emergency workers and woos donors—as well as any number of other urgent tasks—before she falls asleep and does it all again the next day.

Bélizaire, emergency director for the World Health Organization’s Regional Office for Africa, does not expect this work to let up anytime soon. She is on the front line, trying desperately to contain the current Ebola outbreak as it rages across central Africa.

“Our biggest concern right now is that the outbreak is still evolving, and we’re still having a lot of people dying in the community,” she says.

This Ebola outbreak was declared in the DRC in May. By November 17, it had expanded to five countries, with more than 11,600 recorded cases and more than 5,600 deaths. The disease is being driven by a distinct species of virus called Bundibugyo. After a 2014–2016 outbreak of a different Ebola-causing virus in West Africa (in which Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were the hardest-hit countries), this is the second-largest outbreak of the disease in history and the fastest-spreading ever.

Scientists know little about Bundibugyo and how to treat it clinically—but the public health crisis will take far more than medical measures to solve, experts say.

Bundibugyo is a rare species of Ebola-causing virus. It has seen only two previous outbreaks, in 2007 and 2012. Symptoms of Bundibugyo infection, as with other cases of Ebola, include fever, diarrhea, vomiting, headaches and difficulty breathing. Because experts have seen so little of this species of virus before and because the DRC is in social and political turmoil, it’s difficult to determine the exact death rate or how the strain might be evolving.

When virologists were developing vaccines for Ebola during the 2014–2016 outbreak, they did not include Bundibugyo. In primate studies, Bundibugyo appeared less lethal and did not act as fast as other strains, says Tom Geisbert, a virologist at the University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston. Geisbert helped develop the Ervebo vaccine, which treats the Ebola virus (formerly the Zaire virus), a different species than Bundibugyo. Now, Geisbert says, Bundibugyo’s slow-to-appear symptoms mean that asymptomatic people may infect others for days before they are diagnosed themselves.

“We guessed wrong,” he says of the past vaccine effort. “There just wasn’t enough effort put on Bundibugyo to be ready for that.”

Research is now underway on potential Bundibugyo vaccines, including Ervebo, along with a vaccine from the University of Oxford that specifically targets Bundibugyo and an mRNA-based vaccine from Moderna. All three have been approved for a phase 2/3 trial that will test the shots on participants in the outbreak zone. Geisbert says he hopes to see a vaccine approved in the first quarter of 2027.

But many of the reasons for the outbreak’s rapid growth aren’t clinical—and the crisis will not end with the arrival of a vaccine.

Successful treatment for infectious disease relies on contact tracing: accurate tracking of whom a patient could have infected. Right now, about 65 percent of Ebola deaths are happening within community settings, rather than at well-equipped treatment centers. That makes it more difficult to track infected or exposed people’s movements. The DRC’s health ministry recently said that its tracing rate for known contacts had reached roughly 86 percent, but John Johnson, a vaccination and epidemic response adviser at Doctors Without Borders, says he’d be “shocked” if any of the 68 affected health zones in the country were able to track such a high proportion of the actual number of people exposed.

“From what I’ve heard, pretty much everybody says contact tracing is nearly nonexistent in most of these places, and that’s why we’re having so much community death,” he says.

Collecting data is difficult within extremely mobile populations affected by instability. The borders in central Africa are generally porous, and people are constantly traveling across them. The DRC is also facing severe insecurity marked by violent armed conflict across the country, which causes further displacement.

When just one infected person moves, it can start a new chain of transmission—and people are moving by the thousands, says the WHO’s Bélizaire. At the same time, there are more people living in dense urban centers, making the opportunity for spread even greater, she adds.

If and when responders can get a fast-acting vaccine and a handle on contact tracing—and those are big ifs, experts warn—they face communities hardened by years of insecurity and distrust, says Joanne Liu, an epidemiologist at McGill University and former international president of Doctors Without Borders.

Liu visited the DRC several times during a 2018–2019 Ebola outbreak and says she often heard from communities that they had bigger problems than the virus, including malaria, pneumonia, contaminated water and violent attacks. She calls the situation there a “mille-feuille context”—so full of layers and complexity that solutions must start and end with communities themselves.

“What they see is a massive mobilization of aid coming for one specific disease, when actually their challenge is all of the other infectious diseases, plus the insecurity, and nobody is paying attention,” she says.

Liu worries that amid distrust and constant movement, the outbreak could spread farther to places such as the Central African Republic and South Sudan, which have little to no international public health infrastructure, making vaccination campaigns even more challenging.

“It’s one thing to have a vaccine—it’s another thing that it transforms itself into a vaccination. A shot is only good once it’s in people’s arms,” she says.

blocks.text: For Marie-Roseline Bélizaire, a typical day starts around 6 A.M. at a health center in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where she pores over freshly confirmed Ebola cases that have come in overnight. From then on, the work is nonstop: she calls dozens of provinces, visits health centers, supervises contact tracing, trains emergency workers and woos donors—as well as any number of other urgent tasks—before she falls asleep and does it all again the next day.

Bélizaire, emergency director for the World Health Organization’s Regional Office for Africa, does not expect this work to let up anytime soon. She is on the front line, trying desperately to contain the current Ebola outbreak as it rages across central Africa.
“Our biggest concern right now is that the outbreak is still evolving, and we’re still having a lot of people dying in the community,” she says.

This Ebola outbreak was declared in the DRC in May. By November 17, it had expanded to five countries, with more than 11,600 recorded cases and more than 5,600 deaths. The disease is being driven by a distinct species of virus called Bundibugyo. After a 2014–2016 outbreak of a different Ebola-causing virus in West Africa (in which Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were the hardest-hit countries), this is the second-largest outbreak of the disease in history and the fastest-spreading ever.
Scientists know little about Bundibugyo and how to treat it clinically—but the public health crisis will take far more than medical measures to solve, experts say.

Bundibugyo is a rare species of Ebola-causing virus. It has seen only two previous outbreaks, in 2007 and 2012. Symptoms of Bundibugyo infection, as with other cases of Ebola, include fever, diarrhea, vomiting, headaches and difficulty breathing. Because experts have seen so little of this species of virus before and because the DRC is in social and political turmoil, it’s difficult to determine the exact death rate or how the strain might be evolving.

When virologists were developing vaccines for Ebola during the 2014–2016 outbreak, they did not include Bundibugyo. In primate studies, Bundibugyo appeared less lethal and did not act as fast as other strains, says Tom Geisbert, a virologist at the University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston. Geisbert helped develop the Ervebo vaccine, which treats the Ebola virus (formerly the Zaire virus), a different species than Bundibugyo. Now, Geisbert says, Bundibugyo’s slow-to-appear symptoms mean that asymptomatic people may infect others for days before they are diagnosed themselves.
“We guessed wrong,” he says of the past vaccine effort. “There just wasn’t enough effort put on Bundibugyo to be ready for that.”

Research is now underway on potential Bundibugyo vaccines, including Ervebo, along with a vaccine from the University of Oxford that specifically targets Bundibugyo and an mRNA-based vaccine from Moderna. All three have been approved for a phase 2/3 trial that will test the shots on participants in the outbreak zone. Geisbert says he hopes to see a vaccine approved in the first quarter of 2027.
But many of the reasons for the outbreak’s rapid growth aren’t clinical—and the crisis will not end with the arrival of a vaccine.

Successful treatment for infectious disease relies on contact tracing: accurate tracking of whom a patient could have infected. Right now, about 65 percent of Ebola deaths are happening within community settings, rather than at well-equipped treatment centers. That makes it more difficult to track infected or exposed people’s movements. The DRC’s health ministry recently said that its tracing rate for known contacts had reached roughly 86 percent, but John Johnson, a vaccination and epidemic response adviser at Doctors Without Borders, says he’d be “shocked” if any of the 68 affected health zones in the country were able to track such a high proportion of the actual number of people exposed.
“From what I’ve heard, pretty much everybody says contact tracing is nearly nonexistent in most of these places, and that’s why we’re having so much community death,” he says.

Collecting data is difficult within extremely mobile populations affected by instability. The borders in central Africa are generally porous, and people are constantly traveling across them. The DRC is also facing severe insecurity marked by violent armed conflict across the country, which causes further displacement.

When just one infected person moves, it can start a new chain of transmission—and people are moving by the thousands, says the WHO’s Bélizaire. At the same time, there are more people living in dense urban centers, making the opportunity for spread even greater, she adds.

If and when responders can get a fast-acting vaccine and a handle on contact tracing—and those are big ifs, experts warn—they face communities hardened by years of insecurity and distrust, says Joanne Liu, an epidemiologist at McGill University and former international president of Doctors Without Borders.

Liu visited the DRC several times during a 2018–2019 Ebola outbreak and says she often heard from communities that they had bigger problems than the virus, including malaria, pneumonia, contaminated water and violent attacks. She calls the situation there a “mille-feuille context”—so full of layers and complexity that solutions must start and end with communities themselves.

“What they see is a massive mobilization of aid coming for one specific disease, when actually their challenge is all of the other infectious diseases, plus the insecurity, and nobody is paying attention,” she says.

Liu worries that amid distrust and constant movement, the outbreak could spread farther to places such as the Central African Republic and South Sudan, which have little to no international public health infrastructure, making vaccination campaigns even more challenging.
“It’s one thing to have a vaccine—it’s another thing that it transforms itself into a vaccination. A shot is only good once it’s in people’s arms,” she says.
